title: 17. Who May Lead, and Who May Not
purpose: It assembles, from fatwa collections and legal compendia, the rules governing who is qualified to lead congregational prayer, how followers must relate to the imam, and how rows and the placement of women are arranged.

points.text: The section is compiled from a question-and-answer book arranged according to the chapter order of Daʿaʾim al-Islam, supplemented by Mukhtasar al-Musannaf, Mukhtasar al-Athar, al-Ikhtisar, al-Muntakhaba, al-Idah, al-Majalis al-Hatimiyya, al-Majalis al-Mustansiriyya, and epistles of al-Qadi al-Numan and later summoners of Yemen answering Indian questioners.

A list of twelve disqualifications from leading prayer is given: the sick may not lead the healthy, nor the leper, nor one with white leprosy, nor the madman, nor one on whom a prescribed penalty (hadd) has been carried out, nor the child of adultery, nor a bedouin leading emigrants, nor one in fetters leading the unfettered, nor one who performed dry ablution leading those who used water, nor the mute leading those who speak, nor a traveler leading residents, nor one hostile to the Prophet's household leading those who follow it.
The disqualification is relative, not absolute: each of these persons may validly lead others who share his own condition.

Precedence in leading prayer is ranked among seven, per Jafar ibn Muhammad al-Sadiq: earliest in emigration, then best reciter, then most learned in jurisprudence, then eldest; the owner of a mosque has the better right to his own mosque; and the Imam and whomever the Imam appoints outrank all of them.
A woman may lead women in prayer but does not stand ahead of them — they stand to her right and left — and a woman may never stand ahead of a man while he prays behind her.

Recitation that alters the meaning of the Quran voids the leadership: one who substitutes or distorts vowels (e.g. a kasra on the lam in "Allah is free of the polytheists and His Messenger," or a fatha on the ha in "and among them are those whom God guided") may not be taken as imam, must correct his recitation lest he exchange a verse of mercy for one of punishment, and one who does recite well is obliged to lead when the people call him and he is acceptable to them.

Taqiyya licenses modification but not omission of prayer elements: the licensed imam may lower the recitation of the basmala so only he hears it, and may omit "rabbana laka al-hamd" when common people are present — but he must not omit it for any cause other than taqiyya.

A man of the summons who repeats a prayer outside its time purely for taqiyya before those not of the People of the House commits no sin, even if others of the summons follow him with him as their intended imam.

The blind man's imamate is conditionally allowed: al-Ikhtisar permits it when there is need, al-Muntakhaba requires that he be set straight on a given day and sets aside the nasib if he led from the side, and al-Qadi al-Numan wrote that there is no harm if he is set straight — but in every case he is not to be taken as a standing (permanent) imam.

The follower must never precede the imam: he begins each act after him, returns to his prior position if he forgets and precedes, may not stand in front of him (that follower's prayer is void though the imam's is valid), and the Prophet warned that one raising his head before the imam risks having his head turned into a donkey's.

The Prophet, injured by a fall from a horse, led his companions seated and signalled them to sit, then declared that the imam exists to be followed — when he magnifies, magnify; when he recites, be silent; when he says "God hears him who praises Him," say "our Lord, to You be praise"; when he gives the greeting, greet; and when he prays seated, all of you pray seated.

Rank among licensed men governs multiplicity and substitution: two imams are not gathered in one unpartitioned place unless the later is the more excellent; only one granted unrestricted leave may appoint a substitute if his prayer is interrupted; a broken ablution requires appointing a replacement before the imam leaves the mosque or the congregation's prayer is spoiled; and only one whom the summoner designates may step forward to the niche.

Rows must be complete and continuous with the space of a prostrating body between them, none in Mecca closer to the Kaaba than the imam, and a latecomer finding no room prays alone alongside the imam without joining his row — save the imam's hujja, who alone may step level with the imam, by explicit text.

On women praying behind a screen, Sayyidna Jafar ibn Sulayman answers Sayyidna Ali ibn Sulayman that if the place is connected by an opening or lattice the prayer is complete and looking at the men is forbidden before or after entering the sanctified state, cutting off the prayer if directed at non-kin; if the place is not connected, the woman nearest the men takes a single glance at their garments before the sanctified state, and that suffices for all of them — this against the Daudi position that she must keep her gaze on the men during bowing and prostration or none of them has a prayer.
